newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Sen. Chafee sees possible air rule compromise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Sen. Chafee sees possible air rule compromise.

text.p: The chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment Committee said Thursday he believed the Clinton administration and Congress could reach a compromise on the administration's proposed tougher air quality standards.
But Rhode Island Republican John Chafee said he did not have a sense of whether the administration will change its proposal before it sets a final rule on the standards in July.
"I think there's a possibility of perhaps a compromise there," Chafee said at a National Environmental Policy Institute conference.
But asked whether he expected the Environmental Protection Agency to change its proposal to tighten standards against smog and soot pollution, Chafee said, "I don't know."
Under a law passed last year, there is a formal process for Congress to review and vote on the rule the EPA issues.
Chafee said he did not think it was sensible to tighten air quality standards while many communities still were trying to comply with current standards.
But he said there were parts of the EPA proposal that he felt had merit.
"I'm not sure what's going to happen. My crystal ball is very cloudy, so we'll have to wait and see what (EPA) Administrator (Carol) Browner is going to do," he said.
Chafee also said he was "a little surprised" by the severity of the administration's proposal which he said could cost $10 billion annually to implement.

"I don't know if the feeling was that as Republicans we wouldn't want to oppose them because it might look like we're for pollution," he said, noting the last Republican-led Congress took a political bruising for being viewed as anti-environment.
"I've been accused of advocating a shift in EPA implementing the Clean Air Act, and that I view as a standard cost instead of determining it by public health. This isn't so," he said.
But he said he was concerned that "we can't afford these wild, precipitous swings left and right regarding the environment" without losing public support.
"So what I've tried to do is to make sure there is a careful review of science and public health effects and nudging people back to the table and back to the center if possible," Chafee said.
